decision: route the run to figure-it-out, with the Feature playbook as each unit's inner loop
why: nine units on one branch and one pull request is larger than one Feature run, and the multi-phase plan playbook is for many pull requests and does not build

decision: ground the run with the how skill, four read-only Grok explorers (screen, backend patterns, acceptance harness, AI path)
why: the design must start from what the built screen and the shipped backend already do

decision: captured the loop-tier baseline before any change
why: so every later run reads as old value against new value

decision: build a PRD ledger that is not connected to real money: project funds credited by an operator function, holds, per-event settlement at versioned Haiku rates, a separate fee, fractional amounts
why: the ledger and provider-dispatch requirements are unbuilt and available funds always read zero; founder answer: Create a ledger that is not connected to real money transactions

decision: keep decision d100 (PRD tools as an MCP server) and reach it from Anthropic through a tunnel at the integration tier
why: MCP tools are called from Anthropic's orchestration layer even with a self-hosted sandbox, so a local server needs a public address; a local Claude does not serve the Managed Agents API; founder chose MCP server and a tunnel over custom tools on the relay

decision: writers stay on the sheet's Grok row for one small unit first, then fall back to Opus at medium if Grok cancels again
why: Grok writers were cancelled on Windows on 2026-10-16 but the runner has changed since; founder answer: Try Grok once

decision: ran the design arena with five runners from the architect row, each on its own structure: SQL-first authority (Astra), document revisions (Fable), event log (Grok), TypeScript domain core (Opus), normalized tables with a snapshot function (Sol)
why: the data model and authority split is a one-way door for all nine units; the brief asks for a distinct direction per runner

decision: picked the normalized-tables design as the base, with SQL owning every enforced rule; the cross-judge (Sol) scored it 21 of 25, the reducer core 10, the document and event-log designs 11
why: rules enforced in one place that no writer can bypass outranks the reducer's single TypeScript copy, because the reducer's save accepted any state from a service caller

decision: cut the base's storage: one typed document per section version instead of tables for statements, decisions, sources and stories; message parts as jsonb; no recovery worker endpoint
why: no query needs those rows; catch-up on the next send and on a stuck load covers recovery without a scheduler

decision: grafted: one successful commit per turn (Astra), SQL alone prices usage (Astra), sinceSequence 204 polling (Fable), stop only a tunnel the run started (Grok), one TOOLS table and one event mapping for stream and re-read (Opus)
why: each removes a drift or a double path the base left open

decision: read the provider budget as: cap before each turn = session settled spend + this turn's reservation, rounded up to a cent; an overrun is an adjustment that stops admission
why: Managed Agents budgets are cumulative whole-cent caps checked between requests, so a literal per-turn fractional cap is impossible; reversible
